title: Demonstrate an understanding of food or beverage safety practices and procedures in the food or beverage manufacturing environment

lessons.title: Food safety hazards
lessons.html:
Why food safety matters

Every carcass, chicken portion or bag of maize that leaves your plant will be eaten by someone. If it is contaminated, people can become seriously ill or die, the business can lose its customers and licence, and jobs are put at risk. Food safety is everyone's job, from the offloading bay to dispatch.

The three types of hazards

TypeWhat it isExamples in meat and food plants
BiologicalLiving organisms that cause illnessBacteria such as Salmonella, E. coli and Listeria, parasites such as tapeworm cysts, viruses
ChemicalHarmful substancesCleaning chemical residue, veterinary medicine residues, pesticides, lubricants
PhysicalForeign objectsMetal pieces, broken knife tips, glass, plastic, hair, jewellery, bone splinters

How bacteria grow

Bacteria need food, moisture, warmth and time. Meat and poultry are ideal food for bacteria. They multiply fastest at warm temperatures, roughly between 5 °C and 60 °C, which is often called the danger zone. Keeping product cold slows bacteria down; proper cooking kills most of them. That is why chillers, cold rooms and fast processing are so important.

Contamination and cross-contamination

Contamination is when a hazard gets into food. Cross-contamination is when it moves from a dirty item to a clean one, for example:

  • A knife used on the hide is then used on the meat without sterilising.
  • Gut contents spill onto a carcass during evisceration.
  • A worker moves from the dirty area to the clean area without changing and washing.
  • Raw product drips onto ready-to-eat product in a cold room.

Most food safety rules in a plant are there to stop these routes of contamination.

lessons.title: Personal hygiene and good practice
lessons.html:
You are the first line of defence

People carry bacteria on their hands, hair, skin, mouth and clothing. Good personal hygiene stops those bacteria reaching the food.

Personal hygiene rules

  • Wash hands thoroughly with soap and warm water: before starting work, after breaks, after the toilet, after touching your face, hair or phone, and after handling waste.
  • Wear clean protective clothing: overall or coat, apron, hairnet or cap, beard net if needed, and white boots.
  • Keep nails short and clean. No nail polish or false nails.
  • Remove jewellery and watches. They trap dirt and can fall into product.
  • Do not eat, drink, smoke, chew gum or spit in production areas.
  • Cover cuts with a brightly coloured, waterproof plaster so it can be seen if it falls off.
  • Report illness such as diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or infected wounds to your supervisor before starting work.

Hygiene stations

At the entrance to production areas there are boot washers, hand wash basins and hand sanitiser. Use them every time. Do not walk around them.

Knives and equipment

In abattoirs, knives and tools are sterilised in hot water sterilisers between carcasses and when moved from contaminated areas. Follow your plant's procedure exactly. If a steriliser is not working or the water is not hot, tell your supervisor immediately.

Clean and dirty areas

Plants are divided into areas, for example dirty (lairage, stunning, skinning) and clean (dressing, chilling, deboning). Movement should go from clean to dirty, never back, unless you follow the hygiene procedure to change and wash. Colour-coded clothing often shows which area a worker belongs to.

lessons.title: Cleaning, temperature control and records
lessons.html:
Keeping the plant and product safe

Cleaning and sanitising

Cleaning removes visible dirt, fat and blood. Sanitising reduces bacteria to safe levels. Both are needed. A common order is:

  1. Remove loose product and debris.
  2. Pre-rinse with water.
  3. Apply detergent and scrub.
  4. Rinse off detergent.
  5. Apply sanitiser at the correct strength and contact time as on the label.
  6. Rinse if the label requires it, then allow to dry.

Always wear the PPE required on the chemical label, such as gloves, goggles and apron. Never mix chemicals. Keep chemicals in labelled containers, stored away from food.

Temperature control

Your plant will set temperature limits for chillers, cold rooms, freezers and sterilisers. These are critical. Check and record them at the times set out in the procedure. If a reading is outside the limit, report it straight away so corrective action can be taken. Never write down a reading you did not take.

Pest control

Rats, mice, flies, birds and cockroaches spread disease. Keep doors closed, report damaged fly screens, keep waste bins closed and remove waste regularly. Do not touch or move bait stations; these are managed by the pest control service.

Records and traceability

Records prove that food safety steps were done. They also help to trace product back to its source if there is a problem. Fill in records honestly, clearly and at the time of the activity. Sign them.

The law and the inspector

In South Africa, abattoirs operate under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000, and meat inspectors check that hygiene rules are followed. Cooperate with inspectors and follow their instructions.

Key points

  • Food hazards are biological, chemical or physical.
  • Bacteria grow fastest in warm conditions; keep product cold and processing quick.
  • Good personal hygiene and protective clothing stop contamination.
  • Clean first, then sanitise, following chemical labels.
  • Check and record temperatures honestly and report readings outside limits.
  • Records support traceability and prove food safety.
